title: Al-Khwarizmi and algebra
hookLine: the mathematician whose name gives us algorithm and whose book gives us algebra

cards: A man has died and left his estate: some land, some coins, a debt to settle, a bequest to a friend. His widow, his daughters and his mother are waiting.
The Qur'an names their shares in fractions, and somebody has to turn those fractions into actual coins in actual hands, with nobody cheated. Now multiply that by every family in a city.

In Baghdad, a scholar at the caliph's court wrote a short book for exactly this kind of problem. His name was Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi, and a strange word in his book's title ended up in schoolbooks everywhere.

teach.b: The book is usually called the short book on calculating by al-jabr and al-muqabala.
In his opening, al-Khwarizmi says why he wrote it: for what people need every day, in inheritance and wills, dividing property, lawsuits and trade, measuring land and digging canals.
A practical book, full of worked examples. Al-jabr and al-muqabala are two moves.
Al-jabr means restoring, setting right what is broken: when one side of a problem has something taken away, you add the missing piece back to both sides, so the problem is whole again.

Al-muqabala means balancing: when the same kind of thing sits on both sides, you take it off both, and what remains is simpler and still fair. Restore, then balance, and the unknown comes into the open.

The usual account is that Latin readers later kept al-jabr from the title, and it became our word algebra. And dictionaries trace the author's own name, the man from Khwarazm, to our word algorithm, a step-by-step method.

teach.h: WHAT YOU DO TO ONE SIDE, DO TO THE OTHER.
teach.b: The two moves share something with a court of law, or a family dividing an inheritance: whatever you do to one side, you do to the other.
The Qur'an asks people to keep the measure and not cut short the balance.

This week we watched a dynasty fall, a young man escape and start again, a round city rise, and the House of Wisdom gather books on cheap new paper. Here is what grew there: a way of thinking that restores and balances.

how: Muslim scholars working in Baghdad wrote practical mathematics for daily needs, and inheritance law, with its shares named in the Qur'an, was one of the problems their arithmetic served.

o: a judge who settled inheritance cases in Mecca
a Persian poet who wrote verses about the stars
the man from Khwarazm whose book named algebra

p: a problem his book was written for

s: al-Khwarizmi wrote his book as a puzzle for scholars only
his opening says it is for everyday needs: inheritance, trade, lawsuits, land and canals.
setting right what was broken: adding back what one side lost, to both sides.
in his method you may change one side without the other
whatever you do to one side, you do to the other. that is the balance.

games.q: you're al-Khwarizmi. one side of your problem has something taken away from it. what do you do?
o: ignore the missing part and guess.
restore it, adding it back to both sides.
games.why: that is al-jabr, restoring: add back what was taken, on both sides, and the problem is whole again.

practice: Take a pen and any scrap of paper, and write a simple sum with a missing number: something plus three makes ten. Now do the balancing move: take three from both sides, keep the scale level, and write what's left.
Sit with the page and notice its steadiness, one side and the other kept equal; if you pray, you can begin with bismillah, and if not, just breathe with the balance.

wordCard.voice: Al-Khwarizmi. The scholar in Baghdad's House of Wisdom whose book of al-jabr, restoring, and al-muqabala, balancing, gave us the word algebra. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: restoring, setting right. the usual account says Latin readers kept it as algebra.

carryVoice: Your line: restoring and balancing. Fair to both sides, and the unknown comes clear. Day nine hundred seventeen, done.
